quiz.question: Which statement best describes an injection vulnerability?
options: Any request containing punctuation is an attack
Untrusted input changes how an interpreter processes commands, queries, or content
The application accepts a valid Unicode string
The server returns any HTTP error
quiz.explanation: Injection vulnerabilities occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter (SQL, OS shell, template engine, browser DOM) as part of a command or query, altering the intended execution structure.

quiz.question: What is the preferred primary defense against SQL injection?
options: Reject every string containing punctuation
Hide database error messages while retaining unsafe SQL construction
Use parameterized queries and keep user-controlled data separate from SQL structure
Place the database behind HTTPS only
quiz.explanation: Parameterized queries (prepared statements) keep data strictly separated from the SQL code structure. The database engine treats parameter values strictly as literal values rather than executable SQL syntax.

quiz.question: Why is input validation alone insufficient to prevent SQL injection?
options: Valid input can still be inserted into a dangerously constructed query
Input validation always disables database connections
All SQL queries must use operating system commands
SQL databases do not support parameterization
quiz.explanation: Input validation verifies that data conforms to application rules, but if valid input (such as an apostrophe in a legitimate name like O'Connor) is concatenated into a raw SQL string, it will still break the query syntax and trigger injection.

quiz.question: In a React application, which is the safer way to render a plain user-provided comment?
options: Insert the comment directly using dangerouslySetInnerHTML
Render the value using ordinary JSX text interpolation
Evaluate the comment as JavaScript
Disable all browser security headers
quiz.explanation: React's standard JSX text interpolation ({comment}) automatically escapes characters before rendering to the DOM, rendering content strictly as harmless text rather than active HTML markup.

quiz.question: What should be done before constructing a dynamic SQL sort expression?
options: Insert the raw request value into the query
Assume prepared statements parameterize every kind of SQL identifier
Map the requested sort option to a fixed server-side allowlist of identifiers
Remove the database authorization policy
quiz.explanation: SQL parameter placeholders cannot be used for SQL identifiers such as column names or sort directions (ASC/DESC). Applications must map user input to a rigid server-side allowlist of verified column constants.

quiz.question: Which statement about a Web Application Firewall is correct?
options: It can provide defense in depth but does not replace fixing unsafe application code
It guarantees that SQL injection cannot occur
It replaces server-side authorization checks
It makes input validation unnecessary
quiz.explanation: A WAF provides perimeter filtering and defense in depth, but it can be bypassed via encoding tricks or alternative syntax. Remediation must occur at the application layer through parameterized queries and safe APIs.

theorySections.title: Understanding the OWASP Top 10:2025 Architecture
paragraphs: The OWASP Top 10 is the global consensus awareness benchmark for application security risks. The current official release, OWASP Top 10:2025 (the 8th installment), categorizes injection as A05:2025 Injection.

"Injection flaws occur whenever an application constructs executable code or commands by concatenating untrusted data, instead of keeping instructions and data separated through parameterized interfaces."

theorySections.title: Secure Input Handling, Allowlisting, and Schema Enforcement
paragraphs: Input validation is the first line of defense, ensuring that incoming data matches expected types, lengths, ranges, and character sets before the application attempts to process it.
Define exactly what is permitted. If an endpoint expects an interview difficulty, allow strictly ["beginner", "intermediate", "advanced"]. Anything else is rejected immediately.
Attempting to filter out known "bad" characters (like ', --, or <script>) is notoriously fragile. Attackers bypass blocklists via URL encoding, Unicode normalization, or alternative syntax.

A request containing {"reportId": "report-104"} may be 100% syntactically valid, but that does NOT mean the requesting user is authorized to read report-104! Server-side authorization checks must always be performed independently.

theorySections.title: SQL Injection (SQLi) and Parameterized Database Access
paragraphs: SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated directly into a query string, allowing user-controlled input to be parsed as executable SQL syntax by the database compiler.

{`// Vulnerable Node.js SQL const query = \`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '\${req.body.email}'\`; // Attacker input: admin' OR '1'='1 // Resulting query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'admin' OR '1'='1'`} The syntax was altered: the OR statement evaluates to TRUE for every row, leaking the entire database!

{`// Safe Node.js (pg library) const query = \`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1\`; const result = await pool.query(query, [req.body.email]);`} The database driver compiles the query template first. The email value is sent separately as a raw string literal, completely neutralizing injection.
Parameterized placeholders ($1 or ?) only work for values, not SQL identifiers like column names (ORDER BY column) or table names.
Solution: Map user input against a rigid server-side allowlist:

theorySections.title: NoSQL Injection, OS Command Injection, and Template Injection (SSTI)
paragraphs: Occurs when JSON requests supply objects with query operators (like {"$ne": null}) in place of expected strings.
Invoking a shell via exec("ping " + host) allows attackers to chain commands with ; rm -rf /.
Dynamically concatenating user strings into template source allows code execution via {"{{7*7}}"}.

theorySections.title: Secure Output Handling and Context-Aware Encoding
paragraphs: Encoding must match the exact destination interpreter. A value safe for HTML body text is NOT safe inside an HTML attribute, JavaScript block, URL, or CSS style!

theorySections.title: Secure Coding Patterns Across Node.js and React Applications
paragraphs: Modern JavaScript full-stack development provides powerful safe abstractions, but developers can introduce injection through escape hatches.

theorySections.title: Defensive Testing, Code Review, and Why WAFs Are Not the Primary Fix
paragraphs: Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) inspect incoming HTTP packets against signature patterns. While valuable for defense in depth, a WAF is NOT a substitute for fixing vulnerable code. Attackers can bypass WAF regexes using alternative encoding, chunked transfer payloads, or novel syntax.
